strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly stated open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether a single noisy string can strictly reduce generatability (answered affirmatively via Theorem 2.17), and (2) providing a complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability (Theorem 2.19/4.7), which RR25 conjectured might require conditions beyond their sufficient/necessary criteria.

The central technical result (Theorem 2.16, that noise level i ≥ 1 is equivalent to noise level 1 for uniform/non-uniform generation) is genuinely surprising given the contrasting strict hierarchy shown by Bai-Panigrahi-Zhang for generation in the limit without the uniform/non-uniform refinement; this juxtaposition is a nice conceptual contribution showing how the uniform/non-uniform lens qualitatively changes the noise landscape.

The proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained, building carefully on machinery (noisy closure, noisy closure dimension) introduced in prior work, with explicit lemma-by-lemma derivations (e.g., Lemma 3.2's counting argument bounding NC_{i-1} in terms of NC_i) rather than hand-waved sketches.

The resulting characterizations (NC_1(C) < ∞ for uniform noise-dependent generation; a countable increasing union condition with NC_1 finiteness for non-uniform) are simpler and more usable than the original per-noise-level characterizations in RR25, which required checking infinitely many conditions.
The related work section is thorough and situates the contribution clearly within a fast-moving subfield, aiding reproducibility of context even though this is a purely theoretical paper.
weaknesses: The contribution is highly specialized to a narrow and fairly young theoretical subfield (formal language generation in the limit with noise variants); the significance for the broader ICML audience is limited, and the paper does not attempt to connect its stylized combinatorial results back to practical LLM training/hallucination phenomena beyond a brief gesture in the introduction.

The Closing Remarks section is only a few sentences and offers essentially no discussion of limitations, broader implications, or promising directions beyond a generic statement hoping to 'spur future exploration'; there is no discussion of what practical insight (if any) the noise-level-1-suffices result offers for real generative systems.

Some of the combinatorial proofs (e.g., the construction in Theorem 2.17 via Algorithm 1, and the partitioning argument in Lemma 3.2) are intricate and dense, making independent verification by a reader difficult without very careful line-by-line checking; the presentation could benefit from more intuition/high-level proof sketches before diving into the formal argument.

The paper is entirely self-contained theory with no illustrative examples of collections C that instantiate the key phenomena (e.g., no example, however small, is given for Theorem 2.16's equivalence result to build reader intuition, only for the separation in Theorem 2.17), which somewhat hampers accessibility even for a theoretically inclined reader.

The abstract sentence 'Finally, we leverage results to provide the first known characterization' appears to have a typo/missing word ('our results' or similar), suggesting the manuscript could use another proofreading pass.

strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether non-uniform generation is equivalent to non-uniform noise-dependent generation (answered negatively, with a strong separation at noise level 1), and (2) a characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability (Theorem 4.7).

The central technical result (Theorem 2.14) — that generation with any finite noise level i ≥ 1 is equivalent to generation with noise level 1, for both uniform and non-uniform notions — is genuinely surprising given the strict noise-level hierarchy shown for generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026). This nontrivial contrast is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

The core technical lemma (Lemma 3.2), which shows NC_{i-1}(C) ≥ floor(sqrt(NC_i(C))), is a clever combinatorial argument (partitioning and pigeonhole over noisy closures) that cleanly drives the main equivalence result.

The separation construction in Theorem 2.15 (disjoint 'column' languages) is a careful and non-trivial adversarial argument covering multiple exhaustive cases, and it yields a strong result (separation with just a single noisy string).

The resulting characterizations (Theorems 2.16 and 2.17) are notably simpler than prior characterizations from RR25 (reducing an infinite family of conditions NC_i(C) < ∞ for all i to a single condition NC_1(C) < ∞), which is a nice simplification with explanatory value.
weaknesses: The paper is a highly specialized theoretical contribution within a narrow and fast-growing subfield (formal language generation in the limit), evidenced by the large number of very recent, closely related arXiv/conference papers (2025–2026) cited and built upon. Its significance to the broader ICML audience and to practical understanding of LLM behavior is unclear; the connection between 'noisy enumeration' abstractions and real-world noisy training data is asserted in the introduction but never substantiated or discussed further.

There is no empirical or illustrative validation, and more importantly no discussion connecting the abstract combinatorial results back to any practical implications for actual language generation systems, despite motivating language about noisy training data and LLM hallucination in the introduction.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, assuming substantial familiarity with a chain of prior papers (KM24, LRT25, RR25, BPZ26) with minimal self-contained intuition; e.g., Lemma 3.2's proof strategy and Theorem 2.15's exhaustive case analysis are not given intuitive high-level summaries before diving into the formal argument, which limits accessibility.

No explicit limitations section or discussion of the practical scope/boundaries of the noisy-generation model (e.g., is the strict noise-level assumption, unique-string requirement, or countability of the universe restrictive in practice?).

The significance of resolving open questions is somewhat self-referential to a narrow set of very recent papers (mostly 2025/2026, several still in proceedings or on arXiv), so the broader impact and staying power of the specific open questions being resolved is unclear at this early stage of the subfield's development.
